title: Musculoskeletal Pharmacology — Session 1

summary.text: Tissue injury releases **prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines** that sensitize nociceptors; **corticosteroids** block phospholipase A₂ upstream, while **NSAIDs** block COX.

summary.text: **Acetaminophen** treats pain and fever but is not a reliable anti-inflammatory; overdose depletes glutathione so **NAPQI** injures the liver, and **N-acetylcysteine** is the antidote.

**COX-1** is the housekeeping enzyme (gastric protection, renal blood flow) and **COX-2** makes inflammatory prostaglandins; **celecoxib** lowers GI risk but raises cardiovascular risk, with similar renal risk.

summary.text: NSAID harms are **GI, renal, and cardiovascular**; flag anticoagulants, ACE inhibitors/ARBs plus diuretics (**triple whammy**), and corticosteroids — and prefer acetaminophen when red flags stack up.

**OA** is degenerative (treat pain and function); **RA** is autoimmune and needs **DMARDs**, which change the disease course; **methotrexate** is the anchor — **weekly**, with folate, never in pregnancy.

summary.text: **Biologics** target the cascade — TNF (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab), IL-6 (tocilizumab), B cells (rituximab), T-cell costimulation (abatacept) — and all DMARDs share **infection risk**: screen for TB and hepatitis, vaccinate first.

chunks.text: **Nociceptive pain:** direct activation of pain receptors by tissue injury.
**Inflammatory pain:** pain driven by inflammatory mediators.
**Neuropathic pain:** pain from nerve injury or dysfunction.
**Acute pain:** recent onset, often tied to an identifiable injury or flare.
**Chronic pain:** persists beyond expected healing time, often > 3 months. Treatment approach differs sharply between acute and chronic pain.
**Tissue injury → release of inflammatory mediators → sensitization of nociceptors → pain.**
Key mediators: **prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6).**
Arachidonic acid → COX enzyme → prostaglandins → pain and inflammation: the spine of the acetaminophen, NSAID, and corticosteroid sections.
**NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors act at the COX step; glucocorticoids act further upstream; cytokine inhibitors and analgesics act through separate, parallel pathways.**
**Corticosteroids block phospholipase A₂** (membrane phospholipids → arachidonic acid), so a broad range of mediators falls. NSAIDs block only COX, so they lower prostaglandins specifically.
**The immune response:** chronic inflammation involves eicosanoids, leukotrienes, cytokines, chemokines, and many immune cells; RA, SLE, vasculitis, and gout all stem from this cascade.
The lipoxygenase branch of arachidonic acid makes leukotrienes (chemotaxis, bronchoconstriction, vascular permeability) — a separate branch from the COX step NSAIDs block.
Most musculoskeletal pain in this lecture is a mix of nociceptive and inflammatory; pure neuropathic pain belongs to a separate pharmacology unit.
The mediator list is the roadmap for the lecture: NSAIDs target prostaglandins, biologic DMARDs target specific cytokines.

**Therapeutic strategies:** goal 1 is symptom relief and function (NSAIDs and DMARDs); goal 2 is slowing tissue damage, for which DMARDs are absolutely necessary. Response is tracked with indices such as DAS28 in RA.
Corticosteroids (block phospholipase A₂) vs. NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors (block COX): two distinct points of intervention.
Corticosteroids act **upstream** at phospholipase A₂, not at COX — that is why their effect is broader than an NSAID’s.
The lecture’s drugs target nociceptive and inflammatory pain; neuropathic pain is a different unit.
Drug class: Corticosteroids · Step it blocks: **Phospholipase A₂** (upstream) · What falls: A broad range of mediators

chunks.text: Why are corticosteroids broader than NSAIDs? They act at phospholipase A₂, before arachidonic acid is released, so every mediator made from it falls — NSAIDs only stop the COX branch.
Mediators that make pain: **P-B-H-C** — **P**rostaglandins, **B**radykinin, **H**istamine, **C**ytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6).
Effective analgesia, with a narrow margin in overdose: treats pain and fever well, but is **not an anti-inflammatory drug** the way NSAIDs are.
Acetaminophen (the lecture’s single non-NSAID analgesic).
**Analgesic effect:** relieves mild-to-moderate pain, with a central mechanism that is still incompletely understood.
**Antipyretic effect:** reduces fever via central effects on the hypothalamic temperature-regulating center.
**Anti-inflammatory effect:** minimal at the periphery — unlike NSAIDs, acetaminophen is not a reliable anti-inflammatory agent.
Textbook adds: a weak peripheral COX-1/COX-2 inhibitor whose pain relief also involves opioid, cannabinoid, and serotonergic systems.
Reasonable first-line for mild osteoarthritis pain.
Generally safer first-line than an NSAID in a patient with NSAID red flags (kidney disease, anticoagulation, older age).
Preferred over aspirin in aspirin allergy, hemophilia, peptic ulcer history, or aspirin-induced bronchospasm; alone it is inadequate for inflammatory conditions such as RA.
**Overdose: glutathione stores are depleted, NAPQI accumulates, and hepatocyte injury follows.**
Ingesting 15 g may be fatal (centrilobular hepatic necrosis); take care with liver disease, heavy alcohol use, or malnutrition.
**Hidden overdose:** many combination cold, flu, and sleep products also contain acetaminophen — **unintentional double-dosing is a leading cause of acetaminophen-related liver injury.**
Combining acetaminophen with an NSAID improves pain control but can potentiate the NSAID’s GI toxicity.
Normal handling: acetaminophen → NAPQI (toxic metabolite) → glutathione conjugation → safe excretion.
NAPQI = N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine — the “toxic metabolite” example from Lecture 1’s drug-metabolism section.
Mostly conjugated to inactive sulfate and glucuronide; half-life 2–3 hours, relatively unaffected by renal function.
**Always ask about ALL sources of acetaminophen.**
Patients often don’t realize a product contains acetaminophen unless they check the label — reinforce generic-name awareness.
Adults: generally no more than 4 g/day — and even 4 g is associated with more liver function test abnormalities.
**Antidote: N-acetylcysteine**, a glutathione precursor — it replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI.
Case: a patient on regular acetaminophen for back pain starts an OTC cold-and-flu combination. **What is the hidden danger in this combination?** Double-dosing acetaminophen.
**Other analgesics — tramadol:** weak μ-opioid agonist plus serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake inhibition; no anti-inflammatory effect; up to 300 mg/day; risks serotonin syndrome and seizures.
Pain · Acetaminophen: Yes (mild–moderate) · NSAIDs: Yes
Fever · Acetaminophen: Yes (hypothalamus) · NSAIDs: Yes
Inflammation · Acetaminophen: **Minimal — not reliable** · NSAIDs: **Yes — powerful**
Main danger · Acetaminophen: Liver (NAPQI) in overdose or double-dosing · NSAIDs: GI, renal, cardiovascular
Antidote · Acetaminophen: N-acetylcysteine · NSAIDs: Not covered in materials
Why does N-acetylcysteine work? Glutathione is what safely conjugates NAPQI. Overdose uses it up; N-acetylcysteine is a glutathione precursor, so it refills the supply.
Acetaminophen does **P**ain and **P**yrexia, not **P**uffiness (inflammation).
Powerful anti-inflammatory effect, with real systemic risk.
**Nonselective NSAIDs inhibit both COX-1 and COX-2.**
**Celecoxib selectively inhibits COX-2 over COX-1.**
Ibuprofen — common first-line choice for mild-moderate pain.
Naproxen — longer half-life, twice-daily dosing.
Diclofenac — available in oral and topical formulations.
Indomethacin — more potent, more GI/CNS adverse effects.
**Ketorolac — short-term use only, significant GI/renal risk.**
Celecoxib — the COX-2 selective agent.
NSAID → COX inhibition → ↓ prostaglandins → ↓ pain, inflammation, fever.
**COX-1, the “housekeeping” enzyme:** maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow; inhibiting it causes GI and renal adverse effects.
**COX-2:** induced mainly at sites of inflammation and the primary source of inflammatory prostaglandins; selective inhibition targets inflammation with less GI toxicity.
Simplified teaching model, not an absolute separation: COX-1 and COX-2 functions overlap, and COX-2 is also constitutively expressed in the kidney and elsewhere.
Aspirin irreversibly blocks platelet COX (the effect lasts the 8–10-day life of the platelet); other nonselective NSAIDs are reversible inhibitors.
COX-2 inhibitors spare platelet thromboxane (made by COX-1) but block endothelial prostacyclin — so they are not cardioprotective.
Oral NSAIDs for osteoarthritis — effective, but carry the systemic risks below.
Topical NSAIDs — effective local relief with much lower systemic exposure.
NSAIDs ease symptoms but, unlike DMARDs, do not alter the course of any arthritic disorder.
Used in RA, spondyloarthropathies, OA, sprains and strains, low back pain, and gout (tolmetin appears ineffective in gout).
**Gastrointestinal:** gastritis, peptic ulcer, GI bleeding.
**Renal:** decreased renal perfusion, fluid retention, acute kidney injury.
**Cardiovascular:** hypertension, increased risk of cardiovascular events.
**Celecoxib:** lower risk of ulcer/bleeding, but **COX-2 selectivity is associated with increased cardiovascular event risk — a key trade-off.**
Celecoxib’s renal risk is similar to nonselective NSAIDs — COX-2 selectivity does not protect the kidney.
Beyond GI, renal, and CV: headache, tinnitus, dizziness, rare aseptic meningitis, liver test abnormalities, asthma, rashes, hyperkalemia.
Use caution or avoid in: active GI bleeding or ulcer history; chronic kidney disease; heart failure or cardiovascular disease.
Also caution or avoid with anticoagulant therapy and in late pregnancy.
Ibuprofen is relatively contraindicated with nasal polyps, angioedema, or bronchospastic reactivity to aspirin.
NSAIDs + anticoagulants → ↑ bleeding risk.
NSAIDs + ACE inhibitors/ARBs → ↑ AKI risk; add a diuretic and it is the **“triple whammy,”** a very high-yield AKI pattern.
NSAIDs + diuretics → reduced diuretic effect, ↑ renal risk.
NSAIDs + corticosteroids → ↑ GI ulcer risk.
Ibuprofen taken with aspirin blocks aspirin’s irreversible platelet inhibition, limiting its cardioprotective effect.
Celecoxib (a CYP2C9 substrate) occasionally interacts with warfarin and raises lithium and fluconazole levels.
Naproxen’s longer half-life allows twice-daily dosing; diclofenac comes as oral and topical forms.
**Chemistry & pharmacokinetics:** most NSAIDs are weak acids, well absorbed, ~98% albumin-bound, metabolized by CYP3A or CYP2C, and renally excreted.
These three systems (GI, renal, CV) are the organizing framework for every NSAID contraindication and interaction discussion (Table 1).
Highest GI-bleeding risk: celecoxib, or a nonselective NSAID plus omeprazole or misoprostol.
Case: a 72-year-old with OA, CKD, hypertension, and an anticoagulant. **Is an NSAID a good first-line choice for this patient’s pain? Why or why not?**
**Three NSAID red flags at once** — renal disease, anticoagulation, and age-related bleeding risk — make acetaminophen or a non-NSAID strategy generally safer first-line.
Celecoxib is a classic “trade one risk for another” point: a better GI profile, but not a free lunch cardiovascularly or renally.
There is no risk-free NSAID choice, only a different risk profile.
**Choice of NSAID:** all are about equally effective, so choose by toxicity, cost, and patient factors; in renal insufficiency nonacetylated salicylates may be best.
Role · COX-1: **“Housekeeping”** enzyme · COX-2: Induced mainly at sites of inflammation
Protects · COX-1: Gastric mucosa; normal renal blood flow · COX-2: Not covered in materials
Makes · COX-1: Not covered in materials · COX-2: Primary source of **inflammatory prostaglandins**
Blocking it causes · COX-1: GI and renal adverse effects · COX-2: Less inflammation (selective blockade = less GI toxicity)
GI ulcer / bleeding · Nonselective (ibuprofen, naproxen…): **Higher** (Figure 2: 75) · Celecoxib (COX-2 selective): **Lower** (Figure 2: 30)
Cardiovascular events · Nonselective (ibuprofen, naproxen…): Lower (Figure 2: 35) · Celecoxib (COX-2 selective): **Higher** (Figure 2: 65)
Renal risk · Nonselective (ibuprofen, naproxen…): Present · Celecoxib (COX-2 selective): **Similar** — selectivity does not protect the kidney

chunks.text: Why do NSAIDs hurt the stomach and kidney? Blocking COX-1, the housekeeping enzyme, removes the prostaglandins that protect gastric mucosa and keep renal blood flow normal.
Why the “triple whammy”? An ACE inhibitor/ARB, a diuretic, and an NSAID each push kidney perfusion the wrong way at once — together they cause acute kidney injury.
NSAID harms = **GRC**: **G**ut, **R**enal, **C**ardiovascular (Table 1).
**Osteoarthritis (OA):** primarily degenerative joint disease — cartilage breakdown with mechanical wear.
**Rheumatoid arthritis (RA):** autoimmune, systemic inflammatory disease — immune-mediated joint destruction.
OA treatment goal: pain control and function.
RA treatment goal: suppress disease activity, not just pain.
The hinge: OA is managed mainly with analgesics/NSAIDs, while RA requires disease-modifying therapy.
**DMARD (Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drug):** a drug intended to alter the course of RA, not just mask its symptoms.
**Goal of therapy:** slow or halt joint destruction and systemic inflammation, rather than providing analgesia alone.
An NSAID can make a patient feel better without changing the disease trajectory; a DMARD is meant to change the trajectory itself.
Targeted therapy: each biologic class corresponds to a different cytokine or cell type in the inflammatory cascade — the mediator list from the start of the lecture.
DMARD effects take 2 weeks to 6 months to appear. Types: conventional synthetic (cs), biologic (b), and targeted synthetic (ts, e.g., tofacitinib).
Biologics are large molecules, usually proteins made by recombinant DNA technology; JAK inhibitors are oral small-molecule targeted synthetic DMARDs.
**Methotrexate — the anchor drug for most RA regimens.**
Hydroxychloroquine — milder disease; relatively favorable safety profile.
Sulfasalazine — often used in combination regimens.
Leflunomide — alternative when methotrexate is not tolerated.
Adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab — **TNF inhibitors**.
Tocilizumab — **IL-6 inhibitor**.
Rituximab — **B-cell targeted therapy**.
Abatacept — **T-cell costimulation modulator**.
**Mechanism: inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing immune cell proliferation at low RA doses.** (methotrexate)
TNF inhibitors block tumor necrosis factor-alpha signaling.
IL-6 inhibitors block interleukin-6 receptor signaling.
B-cell targeted therapy depletes or modulates B lymphocytes.
T-cell costimulation modulators block the second signal needed for T-cell activation.
Figure 3: abatacept acts at T-cell activation, TNF inhibitors and tocilizumab at cytokine release, rituximab at B cells — all upstream of synovial inflammation and joint destruction.
**OA step 1:** acetaminophen — reasonable first-line for mild OA pain.
**OA step 2:** oral NSAIDs (effective, systemic risks) or topical NSAIDs (local relief, much lower systemic exposure).
**Intra-articular corticosteroid injections:** short-term relief for flares in a single joint.
Other approaches: activity modification, physical therapy, weight management.
Methotrexate anchors most RA regimens; leflunomide is the alternative when it is not tolerated.
Rheumatoid arthritis: they modify the disease course rather than only masking symptoms.
**Glucocorticoid drugs in rheumatic diseases:** used chronically in 30–70% of RA patients; relief is prompt and dramatic, and they slow new bone erosions.
Long-term prednisone in RA: no more than 7.5 mg daily, tapered when possible — even 2.8 mg daily for over 5 years is linked to severe infections.
Intra-articular corticosteroids often relieve painful symptoms for up to several months.
Long-term glucocorticoid harms: osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, Cushing syndrome, infections, cataract, glaucoma, gastric ulcer, depression.
Methotrexate starts at 7.5 mg weekly and rises to 15–25 mg weekly; it slows new erosions in RA.
**Combination therapy with DMARDs** is now the rule when monotherapy falls short; triple therapy (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine) rivals etanercept plus methotrexate.
**Boxed warning — all TNF inhibitors:** possible malignancy, especially lymphoma.
**Boxed warning — all JAK inhibitors:** venous thromboembolism (DVT, PE), major adverse cardiovascular events, and cancer.
Methotrexate key adverse effects: **hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression, pulmonary toxicity.**
**The major safety theme across all DMARDs: immunosuppression → increased infection risk.** This holds for conventional and biologic DMARDs alike.
Methotrexate’s most common toxicities are nausea and stomatitis; dose-related liver enzyme elevations are frequent.
TNF inhibitors: TB reactivation, fungal infections, hepatitis B reactivation, new or worse heart failure, demyelinating disease, lupus-like syndrome.
**Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic).**
Don’t stack biologics: abatacept with a TNF inhibitor probably raises serious infections; upadacitinib with biologic DMARDs is not recommended.
Hydroxychloroquine can reduce methotrexate clearance.
Tocilizumab stimulates CYP450 — doses of cyclosporine or warfarin may need adjusting.
Methotrexate given with TNF inhibitors reduces anti-drug antibodies (infliximab, golimumab, certolizumab).
**Methotrexate is dosed weekly (not daily) — a critical patient-safety point, since daily dosing can be fatal.**
**Folate supplementation** is routinely co-prescribed with methotrexate to reduce toxicity.
**Baseline screening:** e.g., tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C screening before starting biologics.
**Vaccination:** update vaccines, especially live vaccines, before starting therapy.
**Ongoing monitoring:** regular labs to catch cytopenias, hepatotoxicity, or infection early.
**Infection precautions:** counsel patients to report fevers or infection symptoms promptly.
Folic acid or leucovorin reduces stomatitis, GI, and liver test problems but may cut methotrexate efficacy by 10–18%.
Hydroxychloroquine: baseline eye exam, then annual screening after 5 years (retinopathy).
Avoid live vaccines for up to 3 months after stopping abatacept; stop upadacitinib before a live attenuated vaccine.
A 72-year-old with OA, CKD, hypertension, and an anticoagulant: acetaminophen or a non-NSAID strategy first.
OA and RA both affect the joint but are two very different diseases — don’t give RA patients analgesia alone.
Methotrexate’s weekly dosing is one of the highest-yield patient-safety points in all of rheumatology pharmacology.
Match each generic name to its class: adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab (TNF); tocilizumab (IL-6); rituximab (B cell); abatacept (T-cell costimulation).
Topical diclofenac 1% gel is sold over the counter for OA and muscular pain.
**Biosimilars:** near-copies of legacy biologics with the same efficacy, toxicity, and immunogenicity at potentially lower cost.
If methotrexate alone falls short: add csDMARDs or a biologic — usually a TNF inhibitor first, then non-TNF biologics or JAK inhibitors.
Disease type · Osteoarthritis: Degenerative · Rheumatoid arthritis: **Autoimmune, systemic inflammatory**

Drug: **Hydroxychloroquine**, chloroquine · How it works: Suppress T-cell responses and chemotaxis; dampen type 1 IFN · Main uses: Mild RA; SLE (lowers mortality); Sjögren · Watch for: Retinopathy (eye exams); cardiomyopathy; 3–6 months to respond

Drug: **Leflunomide** · How it works: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase inhibitor · Main uses: RA (equals methotrexate) · Watch for: Diarrhea (25%), liver tests, hypertension; half-life 19 days (cholestyramine shortens)
Drug: Azathioprine · How it works: Becomes 6-thioguanine; suppresses B and T cells · Main uses: RA, SLE, transplant · Watch for: Marrow suppression (TPMT, NUDT15), GI upset, cancer, infection

Drug: Mycophenolate mofetil · How it works: IMPDH inhibitor · Main uses: SLE (renal and nonrenal), scleroderma lung; not proven in RA · Watch for: GI, liver, cytopenias, infection; contraindicated in pregnancy

Drug: Cyclosporine, tacrolimus, voclosporin · How it works: Calcineurin inhibitors (block T-cell cytokines) · Main uses: Severe RA; lupus nephritis · Watch for: Nephro-, neuro-, cardiotoxicity, hypertension; CYP3A4 interactions (grapefruit)
Drug: Cyclophosphamide · How it works: Cross-links DNA · Main uses: Lupus nephritis, CNS lupus, vasculitis · Watch for: Cytopenias, infection, sterility, bladder and skin cancer
Drug: Apremilast · How it works: PDE4 inhibitor (↑ cAMP) · Main uses: Plaque psoriasis, PsA, Behçet oral ulcers · Watch for: Diarrhea, nausea, weight loss, mood changes; CYP3A4
Drug: Mesalamine · How it works: Topical colonic 5-aminosalicylate · Main uses: Ulcerative colitis · Watch for: Diarrhea, headache; renal impairment (monitor)

chunks.text: How methotrexate works at RA doses: slides say Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing immune cell proliferation at low RA doses. Textbook says Low-dose methotrexate mainly inhibits AICAR transformylase and thymidylate synthetase, raising extracellular AMP that suppresses inflammation; its dihydrofolate reductase effect is relatively minor at rheumatic doses.
Why can’t RA be treated like OA? RA is immune-mediated joint destruction; analgesics ease pain but leave the immune attack — and the damage — running.
Methotrexate rules = **W-F-P**: **W**eekly (never daily), **F**olate with it, **P**regnancy contraindicated.
Methotrexate toxicity hits **L-B-L**: **L**iver, **B**one marrow, **L**ung.
Why screen for TB and hepatitis first? These drugs suppress the immune response that keeps latent infections in check, so a hidden infection can reactivate.
Generic-name endings: **-mab** = monoclonal antibody (adalimumab, infliximab, tocilizumab, rituximab); **-cept** = receptor-fusion protein (etanercept, abatacept).

2.title: Learning Objectives — Session 1
2.notes: Orient students to the arc of this session: musculoskeletal pain pathways, acetaminophen, NSAIDs, and osteoarthritis/rheumatoid arthritis pharmacotherapy including DMARDs. Tell them this is the first of two sessions on Musculoskeletal Pharmacology — Session 2 picks up with gout, skeletal muscle relaxants, and bone pharmacology on Oct 29.

3.title: Required & Recommended Readings — Unit 2
3.notes: Point students to the required and recommended texts for Unit 2 before diving into content. Katzung’s Chapters 27, 36, and 42 are the required reading for this unit; Pharmacotherapy Principles and Practice is recommended as additional support, not a substitute.

5.title: What Causes Musculoskeletal Pain?
5.notes: Most musculoskeletal pain in this lecture is a mix of nociceptive and inflammatory — pure neuropathic pain is more the territory of a separate pharmacology unit.

6.title: Inflammation Drives Pain
6.notes: This mediator list is the roadmap for the whole lecture — NSAIDs target prostaglandins, biologic DMARDs target specific cytokines.

7.title: Therapeutic Targets in the Pain Pathway
7.notes: This single arrow chain is the conceptual spine for the acetaminophen, NSAID, and corticosteroid sections that follow. The next slide builds this out further with the specific drug classes that intervene at each step.

8.title: The Arachidonic Acid Pathway: Where Analgesics Act
8.notes: This figure adds the drug layer on top of the previous flow slide: name the specific drug classes (corticosteroids vs. NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors) and exactly where each one interrupts the cascade.

10.title: Acetaminophen
10.notes: This is the single most important distinction students need: acetaminophen treats pain and fever well, but it is not an anti-inflammatory drug the way NSAIDs are.

11.title: Acetaminophen Toxicity
11.notes: NAPQI = N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine. Tie this directly back to the "toxic metabolite" bullet from Lecture 1’s drug metabolism section.

12.title: The Hidden Acetaminophen Overdose
12.notes: Good moment to reinforce generic-name awareness from Lecture 1 — patients often do not realize a product contains acetaminophen unless they check the label.

15.title: COX-1 vs. COX-2
15.notes: Stress this is a simplified teaching model, not an absolute separation — COX-1 and COX-2 functions overlap, and COX-2 is also constitutively expressed in the kidney and elsewhere.

17.title: COX-2 Selective Inhibition: Celecoxib
17.notes: This is a classic "trade one risk for another" teaching point — better GI profile, but not a free lunch cardiovascularly or renally.

18.title: Nonselective NSAIDs vs. COX-2 Selective Inhibition
18.notes: This is the graphical version of the trade-off just described in the celecoxib bullet slide — use it to reinforce that there is no risk-free NSAID choice, only a different risk profile.

19.title: NSAID Adverse Effects
19.notes: These three systems (GI, renal, CV) are the organizing framework for every NSAID contraindication and interaction discussion that follows. Table 1.

20.title: NSAID Contraindications & Interactions
20.notes: The "triple whammy" (NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic) is a very high-yield acute kidney injury pattern to flag explicitly.

21.title: Is an NSAID the Right First Choice?
21.notes: Excellent exam-style vignette — ask students to name all three risk factors independently before revealing the answer.

23.title: Osteoarthritis vs. Rheumatoid Arthritis
23.notes: This distinction is the hinge the whole rest of the section turns on: OA is managed primarily with analgesics/NSAIDs, while RA requires disease-modifying therapy.

25.title: What Makes a Drug "Disease-Modifying"?
25.notes: Contrast explicitly with NSAIDs: an NSAID can make a patient feel better without changing the underlying disease trajectory — a DMARD is meant to change the trajectory itself.

27.title: Methotrexate
27.notes: Methotrexate’s weekly dosing is one of the highest-yield patient-safety teaching points in all of rheumatology pharmacology — emphasize it strongly.

28.title: Biologic DMARDs
28.notes: Each biologic class corresponds to a different cytokine or cell type in the inflammatory cascade shown earlier in the lecture — tie this back to the mediator list from Section 1. The next slide shows these same four drug classes as a mechanism diagram.

U2-R1.question: Name the four key inflammatory mediators that sensitize nociceptors and drive musculoskeletal pain.
U2-R1.answer: Prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6).

U2-R2.question: Where in the arachidonic acid pathway do corticosteroids, act compared to NSAIDs? Why does that positioning let corticosteroids suppress a broader range of mediators?
U2-R2.answer: Corticosteroids block phospholipase A₂, upstream of arachidonic acid release, suppressing a broad range of mediators; NSAIDs act only at the COX step, affecting prostaglandins specifically.

U2-R3.question: What is the toxic metabolite responsible for acetaminophen overdose hepatotoxicity, and what is the antidote? Why does the antidote work?
U2-R3.answer: NAPQI; N-acetylcysteine (a glutathione precursor) replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI.

U2-R4.question: Compare COX-1 and COX-2: which one is the "housekeeping" enzyme, and which is the primary source of inflammatory prostaglandins?
U2-R4.answer: COX-1 = housekeeping (gastric protection, renal blood flow); COX-2 = induced at inflammation sites, main source of inflammatory prostaglandins.

U2-R5.question: What trade-off does celecoxib (a COX-2 selective inhibitor) make compared to nonselective NSAIDs?
U2-R5.answer: Lower GI risk, higher cardiovascular risk; renal risk is similar to nonselective NSAIDs.

U2-R6.question: What single feature distinguishes a DMARD from an NSAID in rheumatoid arthritis management?
U2-R6.answer: DMARDs modify the underlying disease process rather than only masking symptoms.

U2-R7.question: Why is methotrexate dosed weekly rather than daily, and what is routinely co-prescribed to reduce its toxicity?
U2-R7.answer: Weekly dosing avoids fatal daily-dose toxicity; folate supplementation reduces hepatotoxicity/marrow suppression/pulmonary toxicity risk.

U2-R8.question: Name one biologic DMARD from each of these categories: TNF inhibitor, IL-6 inhibitor, B-cell targeted therapy, T-cell costimulation modulator. What is the shared major safety risk across all DMARDs (conventional and biologic)?
U2-R8.answer: TNF inhibitor — adalimumab/etanercept/infliximab; IL-6 — tocilizumab; B-cell — rituximab; T-cell costimulation — abatacept; shared risk — immunosuppression/infection.

quiz.stem: A drug blocks phospholipase A₂, so arachidonic acid is not released from membrane phospholipids. Which class is this, and how does its effect compare with an NSAID’s?

options.A: A COX-2 inhibitor, sparing COX-1 housekeeping in the stomach
options.B: An NSAID, blocking the same COX step that celecoxib blocks
options.C: Acetaminophen, acting centrally on the hypothalamus
options.D: A biologic DMARD, neutralizing TNF-α outside the cell
options.E: A corticosteroid, suppressing a broader range of mediators than an NSAID

quiz.why: Corticosteroids block phospholipase A₂ upstream of arachidonic acid release, suppressing a broad range of mediators; NSAIDs act only at COX (S8; SG U2-R2).

whys.A: COX-2 inhibitors act at the COX step, not phospholipase A₂ (S8).
whys.B: NSAIDs block COX, downstream of arachidonic acid release (S8).
whys.C: Acetaminophen acts centrally; it does not block phospholipase A₂ (S10).
whys.D: Cytokine inhibitors act on a separate, parallel pathway (S7).
whys.E: Corticosteroids block phospholipase A₂ upstream of arachidonic acid release, suppressing a broad range of mediators; NSAIDs act only at COX (S8; SG U2-R2).

quiz.label: Q1 · Mechanism · Musculoskeletal Pain & the Inflammatory Cascade

quiz.stem: Which set lists the inflammatory mediators the lecture names as sensitizing nociceptors in musculoskeletal pain?

options.A: Thromboxane, glutathione, NAPQI, and bradykinin
options.B: Prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines
options.C: Prostaglandins, dopamine, serotonin, and insulin
options.D: Histamine, folate, uric acid, and cytokines
options.E: Cytokines, calcium, vitamin D, and histamine

quiz.why: Tissue injury releases prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6), which sensitize nociceptors (S6; SG U2-R1).

whys.A: Glutathione and NAPQI belong to acetaminophen metabolism (S11).
whys.B: Tissue injury releases prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6), which sensitize nociceptors (S6; SG U2-R1).
whys.C: Dopamine, serotonin, and insulin are not on the lecture’s mediator list (S6).
whys.D: Folate and uric acid are not pain mediators in this lecture (S6).
whys.E: Calcium and vitamin D belong to bone pharmacology (S2).

quiz.label: Q2 · Mechanism · Musculoskeletal Pain & the Inflammatory Cascade

quiz.stem: In acetaminophen overdose, why is N-acetylcysteine effective?

options.A: It speeds renal excretion of unchanged acetaminophen
options.B: It blocks COX in the liver and lowers prostaglandin levels
options.C: It is a glutathione precursor that restores NAPQI detoxification
options.D: It inhibits the enzyme that forms NAPQI from the drug
options.E: It binds acetaminophen in the gut and prevents absorption

quiz.why: Overdose depletes glutathione so NAPQI accumulates; N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI (S11; SG U2-R3).

whys.A: The antidote works by refilling glutathione, not by renal excretion (S11).
whys.B: COX blockade is the NSAID mechanism, not the antidote’s (S14).
whys.C: Overdose depletes glutathione so NAPQI accumulates; N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI (S11; SG U2-R3).
whys.D: The lecture’s mechanism is glutathione replenishment (SG U2-R3).
whys.E: The lecture explains the antidote through glutathione, not binding (S11).

quiz.label: Q3 · Mechanism · Acetaminophen

quiz.stem: A 40-year-old with an acutely swollen, inflamed knee asks for the drug that best treats the inflammation itself. Why is acetaminophen not the best choice?

options.A: Its anti-inflammatory effect at the periphery is minimal
options.B: It only works when given intravenously in hospital
options.C: It causes more GI bleeding than the NSAIDs do
options.D: It is contraindicated in anyone with joint swelling
options.E: It has no analgesic effect in musculoskeletal pain

quiz.why: Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever centrally, but its peripheral anti-inflammatory effect is minimal — it is not a reliable anti-inflammatory agent (S10).

whys.A: Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever centrally, but its peripheral anti-inflammatory effect is minimal — it is not a reliable anti-inflammatory agent (S10).
whys.B: No route restriction is taught; it is used orally first-line for mild OA pain (S24).
whys.C: GI bleeding is the NSAID risk (S19).
whys.D: No such contraindication is taught; the issue is weak anti-inflammatory action (S10).
whys.E: It does relieve mild-to-moderate pain (S10).

quiz.label: Q4 · Clinical vignette · Acetaminophen

quiz.stem: Which statement best explains why nonselective NSAIDs cause GI and renal adverse effects?

options.A: They block phospholipase A₂ and stop all mediator release
options.B: They deplete glutathione, which injures the gut and kidney
options.C: They inhibit COX-2, the only source of protective prostaglandins
options.D: They block TNF-α, which normally protects the stomach lining
options.E: They inhibit COX-1, which protects gastric mucosa and renal blood flow

quiz.why: COX-1 is the housekeeping enzyme that maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow; inhibiting it contributes to GI and renal adverse effects (S15; SG U2-R4).

whys.A: That is the corticosteroid site (S8).
whys.B: Glutathione depletion is acetaminophen overdose (S11).
whys.C: COX-2 is the main source of inflammatory prostaglandins (S15).
whys.D: TNF-α blockade is a biologic DMARD mechanism (S28).
whys.E: COX-1 is the housekeeping enzyme that maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow; inhibiting it contributes to GI and renal adverse effects (S15; SG U2-R4).

quiz.label: Q5 · Mechanism · NSAIDs & COX-2 Selective Inhibition

quiz.stem: A patient with a history of peptic ulcer bleeding and no cardiac disease needs an anti-inflammatory for osteoarthritis. The team considers celecoxib. What trade-off must be weighed?

options.A: Lower cardiovascular risk, but higher liver toxicity
options.B: Lower GI risk, but higher cardiovascular risk and similar renal risk
options.C: Higher GI risk, but lower cardiovascular and renal risk
options.D: Lower GI risk, plus kidney protection from COX-2 selectivity
options.E: No trade-off: celecoxib is safer in every organ system

quiz.why: Celecoxib lowers ulcer/bleeding risk but is associated with increased cardiovascular event risk, and its renal risk is similar to nonselective NSAIDs (S17; SG U2-R5).

whys.A: Higher cardiovascular risk is the taught trade-off (S17).
whys.B: Celecoxib lowers ulcer/bleeding risk but is associated with increased cardiovascular event risk, and its renal risk is similar to nonselective NSAIDs (S17; SG U2-R5).
whys.C: Reversed — celecoxib has lower GI and higher CV risk (S17-18).
whys.D: COX-2 selectivity does not protect the kidney (S17).
whys.E: The lecture stresses it is not a free lunch (S17 notes).

quiz.label: Q6 · Clinical vignette · NSAIDs & COX-2 Selective Inhibition

quiz.stem: A patient on lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor) and hydrochlorothiazide starts daily naproxen for knee pain. Two weeks later, creatinine has risen sharply. What pattern explains this?

options.A: The “triple whammy”: NSAID + ACE inhibitor + diuretic causing AKI
options.B: A GI ulcer from NSAID plus diuretic, causing dehydration
options.C: Expected COX-2 renal protection failing under stress
options.D: Hepatotoxicity from NAPQI formed by naproxen metabolism
options.E: Bleeding from the NSAID plus the ACE inhibitor together

quiz.why: NSAIDs with ACE inhibitors/ARBs raise AKI risk, and adding a diuretic is the high-yield “triple whammy” AKI pattern (S20; S20 notes).

whys.A: NSAIDs with ACE inhibitors/ARBs raise AKI risk, and adding a diuretic is the high-yield “triple whammy” AKI pattern (S20; S20 notes).
whys.B: NSAID + corticosteroid raises ulcer risk; this is a kidney injury pattern (S20).
whys.C: COX-2 selectivity does not protect the kidney, and naproxen is nonselective (S16-17).
whys.D: NAPQI comes from acetaminophen (S11).
whys.E: NSAID + anticoagulant raises bleeding; this is a renal pattern (S20).

quiz.label: Q7 · Clinical vignette · NSAIDs & COX-2 Selective Inhibition

quiz.stem: Which nonselective NSAID does the lecture restrict to short-term use because of significant GI and renal risk?

options.A: Diclofenac
options.B: Ibuprofen
options.C: Celecoxib
options.D: Naproxen
options.E: Ketorolac

quiz.why: Ketorolac is for short-term use only because of significant GI/renal risk (S16).

whys.A: Diclofenac is noted for oral and topical formulations (S16).
whys.B: Ibuprofen is a common first-line choice for mild-moderate pain (S16).
whys.C: Celecoxib is COX-2 selective; its trade-off is cardiovascular risk (S17).
whys.D: Naproxen is noted for its longer half-life and twice-daily dosing (S16).
whys.E: Ketorolac is for short-term use only because of significant GI/renal risk (S16).

quiz.label: Q8 · Mechanism · NSAIDs & COX-2 Selective Inhibition

quiz.stem: A patient takes low-dose aspirin for cardioprotection and starts regular ibuprofen for back pain. What is the textbook concern?

options.A: Ibuprofen blocks aspirin’s irreversible platelet inhibition
options.B: Ibuprofen converts aspirin to the toxic metabolite NAPQI
options.C: Both drugs together protect the kidney from injury
options.D: Ibuprofen speeds aspirin’s renal excretion fivefold
options.E: Aspirin makes ibuprofen COX-2 selective, raising CV risk

quiz.why: Concomitant ibuprofen antagonizes aspirin’s irreversible platelet inhibition, limiting its cardioprotective effect (p. 680).

whys.A: Concomitant ibuprofen antagonizes aspirin’s irreversible platelet inhibition, limiting its cardioprotective effect (p. 680).
whys.B: NAPQI comes from acetaminophen (S11).
whys.C: NSAIDs reduce renal perfusion; they don’t protect the kidney (S19).
whys.D: Not the textbook’s interaction (p. 680).
whys.E: Aspirin does not change ibuprofen’s selectivity (p. 680).

quiz.label: Q9 · Clinical vignette · NSAIDs & COX-2 Selective Inhibition

quiz.stem: A 66-year-old has knee pain worse with activity, no systemic symptoms, and mild disease. Which first-line drug does the lecture call reasonable?

options.A: Methotrexate to slow joint destruction
options.B: Acetaminophen for mild osteoarthritis pain
options.C: Adalimumab to block TNF-α signaling
options.D: Ketorolac taken daily as maintenance
options.E: Hydroxychloroquine for mild disease

quiz.why: Acetaminophen is a reasonable first-line for mild OA pain (S24).

whys.A: Methotrexate is the anchor DMARD for RA, an autoimmune disease (S23; S26).
whys.B: Acetaminophen is a reasonable first-line for mild OA pain (S24).
whys.C: Biologic DMARDs treat RA, not degenerative OA (S23; S28).
whys.D: Ketorolac is short-term only (S16).
whys.E: Hydroxychloroquine is a DMARD for milder RA (S26).

quiz.label: Q10 · Clinical vignette · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs

quiz.stem: What is the key difference in treatment goals between osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis?

options.A: OA aims at pain and function; RA aims to suppress disease activity
options.B: OA aims to suppress immunity; RA aims at pain relief only
options.C: RA aims at weight loss; OA aims at infection control
options.D: Both aim only at pain relief with NSAIDs
options.E: OA aims at cartilage regrowth with DMARDs

quiz.why: OA treatment targets pain control and function; RA treatment must suppress disease activity, not just pain (S23).

whys.A: OA treatment targets pain control and function; RA treatment must suppress disease activity, not just pain (S23).
whys.B: Reversed (S23).
whys.C: Neither is the taught goal (S23-24).
whys.D: RA needs disease-modifying therapy (S23 notes).
whys.E: OA is managed mainly with analgesics/NSAIDs (S23 notes).

quiz.label: Q11 · Mechanism · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs

quiz.stem: A patient newly started on methotrexate for RA asks whether to take a tablet every morning “to keep levels steady.” What is the correct counseling?

options.A: Take it daily with food to reduce stomach upset
options.B: Take it daily but skip the folate supplement
options.C: Take it only on days when joints are painful
options.D: Take it once weekly, because daily dosing can be fatal
options.E: Take it twice daily, like naproxen, for steady levels

whys.A: Daily dosing is the dangerous error (S27).
whys.B: Folate is co-prescribed to reduce toxicity, and dosing is weekly (S27).
whys.C: It is a scheduled weekly DMARD, not an as-needed analgesic (S25; S27).
whys.D: Methotrexate is dosed weekly, not daily — a critical patient-safety point, since daily dosing can be fatal (S27; SG U2-R7).

quiz.label: Q12 · Clinical vignette · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs

quiz.stem: What is methotrexate’s mechanism as taught in the lecture, and what is co-prescribed to reduce its toxicity?

options.A: TNF-α blockade; tuberculosis screening
options.B: Phospholipase A₂ blockade; calcium supplementation
options.C: Dihydrofolate reductase inhibition; folate supplementation
options.D: COX-2 inhibition; a proton pump inhibitor
options.E: Glutathione depletion; N-acetylcysteine

quiz.why: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing immune cell proliferation at low RA doses; folate is routinely co-prescribed (S27; SG U2-R7; SG U2-M).

whys.A: TNF blockade is the biologic DMARD mechanism (S28).
whys.B: Phospholipase A₂ is the corticosteroid site (S8).
whys.C: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing immune cell proliferation at low RA doses; folate is routinely co-prescribed (S27; SG U2-R7; SG U2-M).
whys.D: COX-2 inhibition is celecoxib (S17).

quiz.label: Q13 · Mechanism · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs

quiz.stem: A 29-year-old with active RA who is planning a pregnancy needs a DMARD. Which drug from the lecture is contraindicated?

options.A: Celecoxib, because it is a disease-modifying drug
options.B: Acetaminophen, because it is a DMARD
options.C: Sulfasalazine, because it is only used alone
options.D: Hydroxychloroquine, because of its poor safety profile
options.E: Methotrexate, because it is teratogenic

quiz.why: Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy because it is teratogenic (S27).

whys.A: Celecoxib is an NSAID, not a DMARD (S17; S25).
whys.B: Acetaminophen is an analgesic, not a DMARD (S10; S25).
whys.C: Sulfasalazine is often used in combination regimens (S26).
whys.D: Hydroxychloroquine has a relatively favorable safety profile (S26).
whys.E: Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy because it is teratogenic (S27).

quiz.label: Q14 · Clinical vignette · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs

quiz.stem: Which single feature distinguishes a DMARD from an NSAID in rheumatoid arthritis?

options.A: It gives faster, stronger analgesia than any NSAID
options.B: It is always a biologic given by injection
options.C: It changes the disease course, not just the symptoms
options.D: It blocks COX more selectively than an NSAID
options.E: It carries no risk of infection or toxicity

whys.A: DMARDs are not defined by analgesic speed (S25).
whys.B: Conventional DMARDs such as methotrexate are not biologics (S26).
whys.C: A DMARD is intended to alter the course of RA — slowing or halting joint destruction — not just mask symptoms (S25; SG U2-R6).
whys.D: COX blockade is the NSAID mechanism (S14).

quiz.label: Q15 · Mechanism · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs

quiz.stem: Before starting adalimumab for rheumatoid arthritis, which baseline step does the lecture specifically call for?

options.A: Adding an ACE inhibitor to protect the kidney
options.B: Avoiding all vaccines until therapy has begun
options.C: Checking for all hidden acetaminophen sources
options.D: Screening for tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C
options.E: Starting folate to prevent bone marrow toxicity

quiz.why: Biologics cause immunosuppression; baseline tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C screening comes before starting them (S30).

whys.A: Not a DMARD safety step; NSAID + ACEi raises AKI risk (S20).
whys.B: Vaccines, especially live vaccines, are updated before therapy (S30).
whys.C: That is acetaminophen safety counseling (S12).
whys.D: Biologics cause immunosuppression; baseline tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C screening comes before starting them (S30).
whys.E: Folate is co-prescribed with methotrexate (S27).

quiz.label: Q16 · Clinical vignette · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs

quiz.stem: Which biologic DMARD works by blocking the second (costimulatory) signal needed for T-cell activation?

options.A: Rituximab
options.B: Infliximab
options.C: Tocilizumab
options.D: Etanercept
options.E: Abatacept

whys.A: Rituximab depletes or modulates B lymphocytes (S28).
whys.B: Infliximab blocks TNF-α signaling (S28).
whys.C: Tocilizumab blocks IL-6 receptor signaling (S28).
whys.D: Etanercept blocks TNF-α signaling (S28).
whys.E: Abatacept is the T-cell costimulation modulator (S28; S29; SG U2-M).

quiz.label: Q17 · Mechanism · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs

quiz.stem: A patient on a biologic DMARD calls with a fever of 38.6 °C and a productive cough. What lecture principle drives the advice to be seen promptly?

options.A: NSAID-like renal toxicity makes fever dangerous
options.B: Biologics raise cardiovascular risk like celecoxib
options.C: Immunosuppression raises infection risk across all DMARDs
options.D: Biologics cause hidden acetaminophen overdose

whys.B: That trade-off belongs to celecoxib (S17).
whys.C: The major safety theme across all DMARDs is immunosuppression → increased infection risk; patients should report fevers or infection symptoms promptly (S30; SG U2-R8).
whys.D: Hidden acetaminophen comes from combination cold products (S12).

quiz.label: Q18 · Clinical vignette · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs

tree.name: Part 1 · Musculoskeletal Pain & the Inflammatory Cascade

children.name: Key definitions
facts: **Nociceptive pain:** direct activation of pain receptors by tissue injury.
**Inflammatory pain:** pain driven by inflammatory mediators.
**Neuropathic pain:** pain from nerve injury or dysfunction.
**Acute pain:** recent onset, often tied to an identifiable injury or flare.
**Chronic pain:** persists beyond expected healing time, often > 3 months. Treatment approach differs sharply between acute and chronic pain.

children.name: How it works
facts: **Tissue injury → release of inflammatory mediators → sensitization of nociceptors → pain.**
Key mediators: **prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6).**
Arachidonic acid → COX enzyme → prostaglandins → pain and inflammation: the spine of the acetaminophen, NSAID, and corticosteroid sections.
**NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors act at the COX step; glucocorticoids act further upstream; cytokine inhibitors and analgesics act through separate, parallel pathways.**
**Corticosteroids block phospholipase A₂** (membrane phospholipids → arachidonic acid), so a broad range of mediators falls. NSAIDs block only COX, so they lower prostaglandins specifically.
**The immune response:** chronic inflammation involves eicosanoids, leukotrienes, cytokines, chemokines, and many immune cells; RA, SLE, vasculitis, and gout all stem from this cascade.
The lipoxygenase branch of arachidonic acid makes leukotrienes (chemotaxis, bronchoconstriction, vascular permeability) — a separate branch from the COX step NSAIDs block.

children.name: Clinical relevance
facts: Most musculoskeletal pain in this lecture is a mix of nociceptive and inflammatory; pure neuropathic pain belongs to a separate pharmacology unit.
The mediator list is the roadmap for the lecture: NSAIDs target prostaglandins, biologic DMARDs target specific cytokines.

**Therapeutic strategies:** goal 1 is symptom relief and function (NSAIDs and DMARDs); goal 2 is slowing tissue damage, for which DMARDs are absolutely necessary. Response is tracked with indices such as DAS28 in RA.

children.name: Drugs named as examples
facts: Corticosteroids (block phospholipase A₂) vs. NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors (block COX): two distinct points of intervention.

children.name: Exam traps
facts: Corticosteroids act **upstream** at phospholipase A₂, not at COX — that is why their effect is broader than an NSAID’s.
The lecture’s drugs target nociceptive and inflammatory pain; neuropathic pain is a different unit.

children.name: Class
facts: Effective analgesia, with a narrow margin in overdose: treats pain and fever well, but is **not an anti-inflammatory drug** the way NSAIDs are.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Acetaminophen (the lecture’s single non-NSAID analgesic).

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **Analgesic effect:** relieves mild-to-moderate pain, with a central mechanism that is still incompletely understood.
**Antipyretic effect:** reduces fever via central effects on the hypothalamic temperature-regulating center.
**Anti-inflammatory effect:** minimal at the periphery — unlike NSAIDs, acetaminophen is not a reliable anti-inflammatory agent.
Textbook adds: a weak peripheral COX-1/COX-2 inhibitor whose pain relief also involves opioid, cannabinoid, and serotonergic systems.

children.name: Indications
facts: Reasonable first-line for mild osteoarthritis pain.
Generally safer first-line than an NSAID in a patient with NSAID red flags (kidney disease, anticoagulation, older age).
Preferred over aspirin in aspirin allergy, hemophilia, peptic ulcer history, or aspirin-induced bronchospasm; alone it is inadequate for inflammatory conditions such as RA.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **Overdose: glutathione stores are depleted, NAPQI accumulates, and hepatocyte injury follows.**
Ingesting 15 g may be fatal (centrilobular hepatic necrosis); take care with liver disease, heavy alcohol use, or malnutrition.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: **Hidden overdose:** many combination cold, flu, and sleep products also contain acetaminophen — **unintentional double-dosing is a leading cause of acetaminophen-related liver injury.**
Combining acetaminophen with an NSAID improves pain control but can potentiate the NSAID’s GI toxicity.

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: Normal handling: acetaminophen → NAPQI (toxic metabolite) → glutathione conjugation → safe excretion.
NAPQI = N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine — the “toxic metabolite” example from Lecture 1’s drug-metabolism section.
Mostly conjugated to inactive sulfate and glucuronide; half-life 2–3 hours, relatively unaffected by renal function.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: **Always ask about ALL sources of acetaminophen.**
Patients often don’t realize a product contains acetaminophen unless they check the label — reinforce generic-name awareness.
Adults: generally no more than 4 g/day — and even 4 g is associated with more liver function test abnormalities.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: **Antidote: N-acetylcysteine**, a glutathione precursor — it replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI.
Case: a patient on regular acetaminophen for back pain starts an OTC cold-and-flu combination. **What is the hidden danger in this combination?** Double-dosing acetaminophen.
**Other analgesics — tramadol:** weak μ-opioid agonist plus serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake inhibition; no anti-inflammatory effect; up to 300 mg/day; risks serotonin syndrome and seizures.

children.name: Class
facts: Powerful anti-inflammatory effect, with real systemic risk.
**Nonselective NSAIDs inhibit both COX-1 and COX-2.**
**Celecoxib selectively inhibits COX-2 over COX-1.**

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Ibuprofen — common first-line choice for mild-moderate pain.
Naproxen — longer half-life, twice-daily dosing.
Diclofenac — available in oral and topical formulations.
Indomethacin — more potent, more GI/CNS adverse effects.
**Ketorolac — short-term use only, significant GI/renal risk.**
Celecoxib — the COX-2 selective agent.

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: NSAID → COX inhibition → ↓ prostaglandins → ↓ pain, inflammation, fever.
**COX-1, the “housekeeping” enzyme:** maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow; inhibiting it causes GI and renal adverse effects.
**COX-2:** induced mainly at sites of inflammation and the primary source of inflammatory prostaglandins; selective inhibition targets inflammation with less GI toxicity.
Simplified teaching model, not an absolute separation: COX-1 and COX-2 functions overlap, and COX-2 is also constitutively expressed in the kidney and elsewhere.
Aspirin irreversibly blocks platelet COX (the effect lasts the 8–10-day life of the platelet); other nonselective NSAIDs are reversible inhibitors.
COX-2 inhibitors spare platelet thromboxane (made by COX-1) but block endothelial prostacyclin — so they are not cardioprotective.

children.name: Indications
facts: Oral NSAIDs for osteoarthritis — effective, but carry the systemic risks below.
Topical NSAIDs — effective local relief with much lower systemic exposure.
NSAIDs ease symptoms but, unlike DMARDs, do not alter the course of any arthritic disorder.
Used in RA, spondyloarthropathies, OA, sprains and strains, low back pain, and gout (tolmetin appears ineffective in gout).

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **Gastrointestinal:** gastritis, peptic ulcer, GI bleeding.
**Renal:** decreased renal perfusion, fluid retention, acute kidney injury.
**Cardiovascular:** hypertension, increased risk of cardiovascular events.
**Celecoxib:** lower risk of ulcer/bleeding, but **COX-2 selectivity is associated with increased cardiovascular event risk — a key trade-off.**
Celecoxib’s renal risk is similar to nonselective NSAIDs — COX-2 selectivity does not protect the kidney.
Beyond GI, renal, and CV: headache, tinnitus, dizziness, rare aseptic meningitis, liver test abnormalities, asthma, rashes, hyperkalemia.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: Use caution or avoid in: active GI bleeding or ulcer history; chronic kidney disease; heart failure or cardiovascular disease.
Also caution or avoid with anticoagulant therapy and in late pregnancy.
Ibuprofen is relatively contraindicated with nasal polyps, angioedema, or bronchospastic reactivity to aspirin.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: NSAIDs + anticoagulants → ↑ bleeding risk.
NSAIDs + ACE inhibitors/ARBs → ↑ AKI risk; add a diuretic and it is the **“triple whammy,”** a very high-yield AKI pattern.
NSAIDs + diuretics → reduced diuretic effect, ↑ renal risk.
NSAIDs + corticosteroids → ↑ GI ulcer risk.
Ibuprofen taken with aspirin blocks aspirin’s irreversible platelet inhibition, limiting its cardioprotective effect.
Celecoxib (a CYP2C9 substrate) occasionally interacts with warfarin and raises lithium and fluconazole levels.

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: Naproxen’s longer half-life allows twice-daily dosing; diclofenac comes as oral and topical forms.
**Chemistry & pharmacokinetics:** most NSAIDs are weak acids, well absorbed, ~98% albumin-bound, metabolized by CYP3A or CYP2C, and renally excreted.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: These three systems (GI, renal, CV) are the organizing framework for every NSAID contraindication and interaction discussion (Table 1).
Highest GI-bleeding risk: celecoxib, or a nonselective NSAID plus omeprazole or misoprostol.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: Case: a 72-year-old with OA, CKD, hypertension, and an anticoagulant. **Is an NSAID a good first-line choice for this patient’s pain? Why or why not?**
**Three NSAID red flags at once** — renal disease, anticoagulation, and age-related bleeding risk — make acetaminophen or a non-NSAID strategy generally safer first-line.
Celecoxib is a classic “trade one risk for another” point: a better GI profile, but not a free lunch cardiovascularly or renally.
There is no risk-free NSAID choice, only a different risk profile.
**Choice of NSAID:** all are about equally effective, so choose by toxicity, cost, and patient factors; in renal insufficiency nonacetylated salicylates may be best.

children.name: Class
facts: **Osteoarthritis (OA):** primarily degenerative joint disease — cartilage breakdown with mechanical wear.
**Rheumatoid arthritis (RA):** autoimmune, systemic inflammatory disease — immune-mediated joint destruction.
OA treatment goal: pain control and function.
RA treatment goal: suppress disease activity, not just pain.
The hinge: OA is managed mainly with analgesics/NSAIDs, while RA requires disease-modifying therapy.
**DMARD (Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drug):** a drug intended to alter the course of RA, not just mask its symptoms.
**Goal of therapy:** slow or halt joint destruction and systemic inflammation, rather than providing analgesia alone.
An NSAID can make a patient feel better without changing the disease trajectory; a DMARD is meant to change the trajectory itself.
Targeted therapy: each biologic class corresponds to a different cytokine or cell type in the inflammatory cascade — the mediator list from the start of the lecture.
DMARD effects take 2 weeks to 6 months to appear. Types: conventional synthetic (cs), biologic (b), and targeted synthetic (ts, e.g., tofacitinib).
Biologics are large molecules, usually proteins made by recombinant DNA technology; JAK inhibitors are oral small-molecule targeted synthetic DMARDs.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: **Methotrexate — the anchor drug for most RA regimens.**
Hydroxychloroquine — milder disease; relatively favorable safety profile.
Sulfasalazine — often used in combination regimens.
Leflunomide — alternative when methotrexate is not tolerated.
Adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab — **TNF inhibitors**.
Tocilizumab — **IL-6 inhibitor**.
Rituximab — **B-cell targeted therapy**.
Abatacept — **T-cell costimulation modulator**.

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **Mechanism: inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing immune cell proliferation at low RA doses.** (methotrexate)
TNF inhibitors block tumor necrosis factor-alpha signaling.
IL-6 inhibitors block interleukin-6 receptor signaling.
B-cell targeted therapy depletes or modulates B lymphocytes.
T-cell costimulation modulators block the second signal needed for T-cell activation.
Figure 3: abatacept acts at T-cell activation, TNF inhibitors and tocilizumab at cytokine release, rituximab at B cells — all upstream of synovial inflammation and joint destruction.

children.name: Indications
facts: **OA step 1:** acetaminophen — reasonable first-line for mild OA pain.
**OA step 2:** oral NSAIDs (effective, systemic risks) or topical NSAIDs (local relief, much lower systemic exposure).
**Intra-articular corticosteroid injections:** short-term relief for flares in a single joint.
Other approaches: activity modification, physical therapy, weight management.
Methotrexate anchors most RA regimens; leflunomide is the alternative when it is not tolerated.
Rheumatoid arthritis: they modify the disease course rather than only masking symptoms.
**Glucocorticoid drugs in rheumatic diseases:** used chronically in 30–70% of RA patients; relief is prompt and dramatic, and they slow new bone erosions.
Long-term prednisone in RA: no more than 7.5 mg daily, tapered when possible — even 2.8 mg daily for over 5 years is linked to severe infections.
Intra-articular corticosteroids often relieve painful symptoms for up to several months.
Long-term glucocorticoid harms: osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, Cushing syndrome, infections, cataract, glaucoma, gastric ulcer, depression.
Methotrexate starts at 7.5 mg weekly and rises to 15–25 mg weekly; it slows new erosions in RA.
**Combination therapy with DMARDs** is now the rule when monotherapy falls short; triple therapy (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine) rivals etanercept plus methotrexate.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **Boxed warning — all TNF inhibitors:** possible malignancy, especially lymphoma.
**Boxed warning — all JAK inhibitors:** venous thromboembolism (DVT, PE), major adverse cardiovascular events, and cancer.
Methotrexate key adverse effects: **hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression, pulmonary toxicity.**
**The major safety theme across all DMARDs: immunosuppression → increased infection risk.** This holds for conventional and biologic DMARDs alike.
Methotrexate’s most common toxicities are nausea and stomatitis; dose-related liver enzyme elevations are frequent.
TNF inhibitors: TB reactivation, fungal infections, hepatitis B reactivation, new or worse heart failure, demyelinating disease, lupus-like syndrome.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: **Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic).**
Don’t stack biologics: abatacept with a TNF inhibitor probably raises serious infections; upadacitinib with biologic DMARDs is not recommended.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: Hydroxychloroquine can reduce methotrexate clearance.
Tocilizumab stimulates CYP450 — doses of cyclosporine or warfarin may need adjusting.
Methotrexate given with TNF inhibitors reduces anti-drug antibodies (infliximab, golimumab, certolizumab).

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: **Methotrexate is dosed weekly (not daily) — a critical patient-safety point, since daily dosing can be fatal.**

children.name: Monitoring
facts: **Folate supplementation** is routinely co-prescribed with methotrexate to reduce toxicity.
**Baseline screening:** e.g., tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C screening before starting biologics.
**Vaccination:** update vaccines, especially live vaccines, before starting therapy.
**Ongoing monitoring:** regular labs to catch cytopenias, hepatotoxicity, or infection early.
**Infection precautions:** counsel patients to report fevers or infection symptoms promptly.
Folic acid or leucovorin reduces stomatitis, GI, and liver test problems but may cut methotrexate efficacy by 10–18%.
Hydroxychloroquine: baseline eye exam, then annual screening after 5 years (retinopathy).
Avoid live vaccines for up to 3 months after stopping abatacept; stop upadacitinib before a live attenuated vaccine.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: A 72-year-old with OA, CKD, hypertension, and an anticoagulant: acetaminophen or a non-NSAID strategy first.
OA and RA both affect the joint but are two very different diseases — don’t give RA patients analgesia alone.
Methotrexate’s weekly dosing is one of the highest-yield patient-safety points in all of rheumatology pharmacology.
Match each generic name to its class: adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab (TNF); tocilizumab (IL-6); rituximab (B cell); abatacept (T-cell costimulation).
Topical diclofenac 1% gel is sold over the counter for OA and muscular pain.
**Biosimilars:** near-copies of legacy biologics with the same efficacy, toxicity, and immunogenicity at potentially lower cost.
If methotrexate alone falls short: add csDMARDs or a biologic — usually a TNF inhibitor first, then non-TNF biologics or JAK inhibitors.
